before.title: A340E Automatic Transmission Wear (Overdrive Slip / Torque-Converter Shudder)
before.description: The 4-speed A340E automatic in the SC300 is durable but, on neglected examples, begins showing age around 130,000-150,000 miles: slipping out of overdrive, delayed engagement, and a shudder at highway speed from a worn torque-converter lockup clutch. The valve body and shift solenoids degrade from heat cycling, and most used SC300s have never had a proper fluid/filter service, which accelerates the wear. No recalls are tied to this; it is age/maintenance related.
before.solution: Perform a proper fluid and filter service using Toyota Type T-IV ATF as preventive care. If shudder/slip is already present, address the torque converter, valve body, and shift solenoids; a full A340E rebuild (roughly $1,800-$2,500) is the fix for advanced wear.
symptoms: Harsh or delayed shifting when cold

citations.title: Wont Shift into Overdrive - ClubLexus

proposal.title: A340E Automatic Transmission Wear (Overdrive Slip / Torque-Converter Shudder)
proposal.description: Two direct SC300 threads document intermittent or absent overdrive, but both ultimately point away from the frozen A340E-wear diagnosis: one 1995 owner reported an ECU replacement restored overdrive after a fluid/filter service did not, and one 1993 owner reported the same after ECU refurbishment failed while a replacement ECU succeeded. A second owner in that discussion said a transmission rebuild did not correct a similar condition. These sources do not establish wear at 130,000-150,000 miles, torque-converter shudder, valve-body or solenoid degradation, neglected service prevalence, or a rebuild as the default fix.
proposal.solution: Scan transmission and engine controls, verify coolant-temperature, speed, throttle and overdrive-switch inputs, inspect wiring and ECU function, and perform the model-year repair-manual hydraulic and electrical tests before condemning the transmission. Use only the exact model-year fluid specification and level procedure. Do not prescribe a converter, valve body, solenoids or rebuild from an overdrive symptom alone. This is diagnosis- and model-year-specific transmission-control work; no universal ATF, ECU, torque converter, valve body, solenoid, rebuild kit or retail part is asserted.

before.title: Distributor Cap & Rotor Cracking / Ignition Misfire (Non-VVT-i 1992-1997)
before.description: Pre-VVT-i 2JZ-GE SC300s (1992-1997) use a cam-driven distributor. With age the cap and rotor crack; spark then jumps through the crack, burning a hole in the rotor and causing misfires, rough cold idle, and shaking at idle. A leaking valve-cover gasket that lets oil pool in the spark-plug tubes produces overlapping misfire symptoms, so both should be inspected together. (The 1998-2000 VVT-i engine is distributorless with individual coils, so this applies only to the non-VVT-i years.)
before.solution: Replace the distributor cap and rotor (or a good remanufactured distributor if the shaft/bearing is worn); replace the valve cover gasket and spark-plug tube seals if oil is present in the plug wells, and inspect/clean the throttle body. Replace brittle plug wires as preventive maintenance.
symptoms: Oil in spark-plug tubes (related valve-cover leak)

citations.title: Ignition Distributor Cap And Rotor - Lexus Owners Club

proposal.title: Distributor Cap & Rotor Cracking / Ignition Misfire (Non-VVT-i 1992-1997)
proposal.description: One direct report supports repeated distributor-rotor cracking and idle misfire on a 1992 SC300, beginning after distributor O-ring service. The owner found no obvious shaft play, and the only proposed cause in the thread was possible post-service misalignment. The source does not establish an age-driven 1992-1997 pattern or prove that valve-cover leakage, plug wires, spark-plug-tube oil or throttle deposits caused the same event.
proposal.solution: Diagnose the misfire and inspect the cap, rotor, distributor alignment, shaft condition, plugs, wires and plug wells separately. Replace a cap or rotor only when cracking, tracking or wear is confirmed; correct oil leakage or distributor mechanical damage only at its verified source. This is year- and diagnosis-specific ignition work; no universal cap, rotor, distributor, wire set, gasket, seal or retail part is asserted.

before.title: Front Lower Control Arm Bushing & Ball Joint Wear (Clunk Over Bumps)
before.description: The front lower control arm rubber bushings wear out with age, allowing slop that produces a clunk or knock over bumps and during rapid speed changes, plus vague steering. On the SC, the lower ball joint is integral to the control arm and is not separately serviceable, so a worn ball joint requires the whole arm. Supra MkIV (JZA80) lower control arms interchange and are often cheaper than Lexus units; polyurethane bushing kits are also available.
before.solution: Replace worn bushings (OEM rubber or polyurethane) to eliminate the clunk; if the integral ball joint is also worn, replace the complete lower control arm assembly (later-gen Supra arms interchange; note JZA70 arms do NOT fit). Do both sides and align afterward.

proposal.title: Front Lower Control Arm Bushing & Ball Joint Wear (Clunk Over Bumps)
proposal.description: Lexus communication PG012-02 establishes an on-vehicle ball-joint inspection method for 1992-2000 SC300 and SC400 vehicles, but it does not declare common bushing or ball-joint failure or identify clunking as proof of one part. A direct owner report documents diagnosed bad ball joints on one 1999 SC300 and successful installation of specified 1993-1996 Supra lower arms. That single fitment does not prove that every Supra arm, every SC model year or every bushing option is interchangeable.
proposal.solution: Inspect the complete front suspension using the Lexus ball-joint play procedure and isolate the clunk before replacing parts. If a lower arm or its non-serviceable joint is outside specification, verify the exact left/right arm by VIN and current catalog supersession; do not generalize one owner’s Supra interchange result to every 1992-2000 SC300/SC400. Align the vehicle after an arm replacement when the repair procedure requires it. This is VIN-, side- and inspection-specific suspension work; no universal control arm, bushing, ball joint, Supra interchange or retail part is asserted.

before.title: Power Steering Pump Seal Leak Contaminating the Alternator
before.description: The power steering pump on the first-gen SC develops a faulty seal that leaks power steering fluid. Because the alternator sits directly below the pump, the fluid can drip onto it. If neglected, the fluid saturates and destroys the alternator, turning a modest seal leak into a two-part failure. This is a widely cited SC300/SC400 (and shared LS400) age-related issue; the pump seals and pressure valve commonly fail from heat past ~100k miles.
before.solution: Reseal or replace the power steering pump before fluid reaches the alternator; clean/inspect the alternator, and replace it if already fluid-soaked. Address the pressure control valve if it is the leak source. Doing both the pump and alternator together is common practice when the alternator is contaminated.
symptoms: Power steering fluid leak / low reservoir

proposal.title: Power Steering Pump Seal Leak Contaminating the Alternator

A separate SC300 report traced alternator-damaging engine oil to the distributor area. The reviewed evidence therefore does not establish a recurring SC300 pump-seal path onto the alternator, a 100,000-mile threshold, shared LS400 behavior, or one pressure-valve cause.
proposal.solution: Identify the fluid, clean the area and locate the highest active wet point before replacing anything; inspect the distributor area, power-steering reservoir, pump, hoses and fittings as separate possible sources. Test alternator output and contamination rather than replacing it automatically with the pump. This is fluid-, source- and diagnosis-specific work; no universal pump, seal kit, pressure valve, alternator or retail part is asserted.

before.title: Power Window Regulator Nylon Carrier Failure
before.description: The SC300/SC400 door window regulators use a plastic/nylon carrier that holds a steel block on the lift cable. With age the nylon cracks and the ears break, allowing the steel block to tear through the guide. The glass then goes crooked, drops into the door, or the motor spins without moving the window. A clicking or POP sound during window travel is the classic early warning. Aggravated by dried outer window sweep rubber that drags on the glass.
before.solution: Replace the window regulator (OEM or quality aftermarket); replace the dried/worn outer window sweeps to reduce drag. Temporary adhesive/J-B Weld repairs of the carrier are known to fail after only a handful of cycles; durable DIY fixes reinforce the nylon carrier with drilled holes and metal.
symptoms: Clicking or pop sound when window moves
Window sits crooked in the track
Glass drops into door and won't return
Motor runs but window doesn't move

proposal.title: Power Window Regulator Nylon Carrier Failure
proposal.description: A direct 1992 SC owner documented the regulator cable’s metal block tearing through a cracked white plastic guide, allowing the window to stop moving correctly. That report supports a real carrier failure mechanism, but not a generation-wide failure rate, one universal clicking or pop warning, or dried outer sweeps as the cause in every vehicle.
proposal.solution: Secure the glass and distinguish switch, motor, cable, guide and regulator faults before ordering parts. If the carrier or cable has failed, replace the exact side-specific regulator assembly or use a qualified repair that preserves cable alignment and glass travel; inspect guides and weatherstrips only for measured binding or damage. This is side-, condition- and fitment-specific window repair; no universal regulator, motor, carrier, sweep, adhesive repair or retail part is asserted.

before.title: VVT-i Cam Gear O-Ring / Intake Cam Seal Oil Leak (1998-2000 VVT-i 2JZ-GE)
before.description: On the VVT-i version of the 2JZ-GE (introduced on the SC300 for the 1998 model year and produced through the end of the run in 2000), the intake cam VVT-i gear/actuator uses an internal O-ring that hardens with age and heat, allowing oil to weep from the front of the cylinder head near the timing cover. It is one of the most commonly reported oil leaks on high-mileage VVT-i 2JZ-GE engines (shared with the GS300/IS300 siblings). Toyota advises against disassembling the VVT-i gear (gear backlash risk), so many owners address it by replacing the O-ring with an aftermarket Viton/FKM kit or replacing the front cam seal.
before.solution: Replace the VVT-i cam gear O-ring (aftermarket Viton/FKM rebuild kit) and/or the front intake camshaft oil seal. Inspect the timing-belt-area seals at the same time and replace the timing belt if due since access overlaps. Use OEM or high-temp Viton seals to prevent recurrence. Dealers typically only sell the complete VVT-i gear (~$350) rather than the O-ring alone.
symptoms: Oil weeping/dripping from front of engine near timing cover
Oil residue on lower front of block

citations.title: VVTi cam gear leaking oil - Lexus IS Forum (my.is)

proposal.title: VVT-i Cam Gear O-Ring / Intake Cam Seal Oil Leak (1998-2000 VVT-i 2JZ-GE)
proposal.description: Direct reports from 1998 and 1999 SC300 owners document oil at the VVT-i gear and timing-cover area. They support the symptom and frozen VVT-i year boundary, but do not by themselves prove whether the leak comes from an internal gear O-ring, the front camshaft seal, cam-cap sealant or another nearby source. No reviewed primary source supports the frozen prevalence, a Toyota warning against disassembly, an aftermarket Viton/FKM repair, complete-gear price or automatic timing-belt replacement.
proposal.solution: Clean the area and trace fresh oil from its highest point, using dye if needed, before disturbing the timing system. If the VVT-i gear, camshaft seal or another seal is confirmed, follow the exact model-year repair manual and inspect the timing belt for oil contamination or service due status; do not open the gear or bundle unrelated parts without an approved procedure. This is leak-source- and procedure-specific engine work; no universal O-ring, cam gear, cam seal, timing belt, kit or retail part is asserted.
